stem: (a) A cake of size1 is divided among n>1 people. Is equal division the only Pareto-optimal allocation? (b) Classify these transactions for GDP and consumption/investment: paying someone for cooking and cleaning at home; buying a new car for personal use; flying Delhi–Kolkata to attend Durga Puja; buying100 company shares directly online; building a house.
answer: (a) No: every complete allocation is Pareto optimal if each person prefers more cake. (b) Paid domestic services, personal car and personal flight are consumption; share purchase is excluded as a financial transaction; new-house construction is residential investment.
solution: (a) With strictly increasing individual utility in own cake, all allocations xᵢ≥0 with Σxᵢ=1 are efficient: giving someone more requires taking cake from someone else. Equal division is one efficient allocation, but so is giving all cake to one person. Equity and Pareto efficiency are different criteria. (b) Paid cooking/cleaning is a newly produced household service and counts as consumption, unlike unpaid own-household work. A new personal car is consumer-durable consumption; a leisure flight is service consumption. Buying existing or newly issued shares changes financial ownership and is not purchase of current final output; separately charged brokerage services can enter GDP. Construction of a new house is fixed residential investment, even when bought for the owner’s personal use. Imported content is offset through imports in domestic GDP.
hint: Efficiency asks whether any improvement is possible, not whether shares are equal; distinguish real production from financial transactions.
notes: Subpart (b) is national-income accounting; ordinary domestic production and strictly increasing preferences in cake are assumed.

stem: Roses must be sold on the day they bloom. Growing costs are already sunk; demand is P=α−Q, α>0. (a) A monopolist has1000 roses: find sales and price. (b) Ten sellers each have100 roses, α≥1100: find equilibrium. (c) Numerous price-taking sellers have1000 roses in total: find competitive sales and price.
answer: (a) Q=min(α/2,1000), P=α−Q. (b) Under capacity-constrained Cournot competition all sell100: Q1000,P=α−1000. (c) Q=min(α,1000), P=max(α−1000,0).
solution: (a) With no avoidable growing cost, maximize (α−Q)Q over0≤Q≤1000; the unconstrained maximizer is α/2. (b) If each seller takes rival quantities as fixed, best response is qᵢ=min(100,max(0,(α−Q_−i)/2)). At rivals’ total900, α≥1100 implies the desired quantity is at least100, so all capacities bind. The symmetric equilibrium has total1000 and priceα−1000. (c) Price-taking sellers offer their available roses whenever price is positive. If α≥1000, all1000 sell atα−1000. If0<α<1000, market-clearing consumption isα at zero price, with surplus roses unsold or discarded. At α=1000 price is zero and full supply can be absorbed.
hint: Sunk growing costs do not enter the day’s sales decision, but physical capacities do.
notes: Part (b) uses the standard Cournot interpretation for ten strategic sellers; the source does not explicitly name their strategic choice variable.

stem: Laxmi buys rice, cabbage and potatoes. On very low-income days she buys only rice; she never buys vegetables without rice. When she buys vegetables, she chooses only the cheaper vegetable per kg. Vegetable prices vary; rice price is fixed. Give a suitable utility function and explain.
answer: One example is U(r,c,p)=r exp[β(c+p)], β>0, for nonnegative quantities.
solution: For r>0 this represents the same preferences as log r+β(c+p). Cabbage and potatoes are perfect substitutes, so with unequal prices any vegetable spending goes to the cheaper one. Let its price be v and rice price be p_r. Maximize log r+βz subject to p_rr+vz=M. If M≤v/β, the optimum is r=M/p_r,z=0: low income goes entirely to rice. If M>v/β, the optimum is r=v/(βp_r)>0 and z=(M−v/β)/v>0. Zero rice yields U=0, whereas any positive rice with M>0 gives positive utility, so a vegetable-only bundle is never optimal. Equal vegetable prices allow either vegetable or mixtures; the source only requires choice of the cheaper when prices differ. This is an example, not a uniquely identified preference representation.
hint: Make vegetables perfect substitutes and give rice very high marginal utility near zero.

stem: In a closed Keynesian economy without government, saving is initially proportional to income and the marginal propensity to invest is0.3. After a parallel downward shift in saving, equilibrium saving increases by12. Find the income change.
solution: At both equilibria saving equals investment. Therefore the observed change in equilibrium saving12 equals the change in investment. The investment schedule is unchanged and ΔI=.3ΔY, so ΔY=12/.3=40. The size of the downward saving shift and the initial saving propensity are not needed. A stable standard model would also require the marginal propensity to save to exceed .3.
hint: Use equilibrium S=I before and after the shift.

stem: IS–LM has C=a+bY, a>0,0<b<1, exogenous I₀,G₀ and money demand L=kY−gr, k,g>0. Nominal money is M₀, initial price P₀. (i) Set up equilibrium equations. (ii) How does a rise to P₁>P₀ affect Y and r?
answer: Y*=(a+I₀+G₀)/(1−b), unchanged by the price rise. r*=[kY*−M₀/P]/g rises by(M₀/g)(1/P₀−1/P₁).
solution: IS is Y=a+bY+I₀+G₀, fixing output regardless of interest because investment is exogenous. It is vertical in the usual(Y,r) plane. LM is M₀/P=kY−gr, or r=(kY−M₀/P)/g. A higher price lowers real money supply and shifts LM upward/leftward. Its intersection with the vertical IS therefore has the same Y and a higher r, with the exact increase given above. There is no investment crowding-out channel in this particular specification.
hint: Notice that no goods-market component depends on interest.
